title: Threat Modelling
objectives: Draw a system’s trust boundaries and data flows
Use STRIDE to list threats at each boundary
Rank threats and choose mitigations before writing code

cards.title: Four questions before any control
cards.body: Threat modelling asks: what are we building, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, and did we do a good job? Answering them on a whiteboard before coding is cheaper than discovering the answers in an incident review.

cards.title: Trust boundaries are where attacks happen
cards.body: A trust boundary is a line data crosses between parts with different privileges: browser to server, service to database, your code to a third-party API. Input crossing a boundary inward must be checked; secrets crossing outward must not leak. Most real vulnerabilities sit on one of these lines.

cards.title: Worked example: STRIDE on a file-upload feature
cards.body: Walk one data flow, a user uploading a profile picture, through the six STRIDE categories.
steps: Spoofing: can someone upload as another user? Require an authenticated session on the upload endpoint
Tampering: can the file be changed in transit or storage? Use TLS and write-once object storage
Repudiation: can a user deny uploading abuse? Log uploader id, time and file hash
Information disclosure: can others read private uploads? Serve them through signed, expiring URLs
Denial of service: can huge files exhaust storage? Cap size and rate per user
Elevation of privilege: can a crafted file run code? Never execute uploads; re-encode images in a sandboxed worker

cards.title: Misconception: security is a feature added at the end
cards.body: Controls bolted on after design tend to miss whole data flows, such as an admin export or a webhook nobody listed. Modelling while designing finds those paths when changing them costs a diagram edit, not a migration.

cards.title: Trap: modelling only the happy path
cards.body: Diagrams often show the main request path and omit support tools, batch jobs, backups and CI credentials. Attackers look for exactly those side doors. Include every way data enters, leaves or is stored, including operational access.

questions.prompt: Where should input validation for a public API be enforced?

choices.label: In the mobile app before it sends requests
At the CDN, with a cache rule per route
In the web form, with the rules documented
Where requests cross into the server

questions.explanation: Clients and their forms are outside the trust boundary and can be bypassed by calling the API directly. A CDN caches responses; it does not validate input. The server boundary is the first point you control.

questions.prompt: An attacker edits a price field in a signed-out cart cookie. Which STRIDE category is this?

choices.label: Tampering
Repudiation
Denial of service
Spoofing

questions.explanation: Changing data the system relies on is tampering; sign or keep it server-side.

questions.prompt: A user claims they never approved a payout, and there is no record either way. Which threat was left open?

choices.label: Tampering
Information disclosure
Spoofing
Repudiation

questions.explanation: Without trustworthy audit logs, actions can be denied.

questions.prompt: Which item is most often missing from a first data-flow diagram?

choices.label: The external payment provider
The login and sign-up flows
The primary database and its replicas
Admin tools and batch jobs

questions.explanation: Operational side paths such as admin tools and batch jobs are easy to forget and attractive to attackers. The main user flows, the primary database and third-party providers are what people draw first.

questions.prompt: A small team adds a feature that lets customers connect their accounting software via webhooks.

Ship, then commission a penetration test next quarter
A one-hour STRIDE pass on the new data flows before building

Finds design-level issues while they are cheap to change
More pages mean more security
Fits the deadline and the team’s size

mechanism.title: From a diagram to a list of mitigations
steps: Start with a data-flow diagram: external actors (users, partners), processes (services, jobs), data stores and the flows between them. Keep it to one page; a diagram nobody can read in five minutes will not be reviewed.

Draw trust boundaries wherever privilege changes: the internet edge, the line between a service and its database, between tenants, and around anything run by a third party. Each flow that crosses a boundary is a candidate attack path.

Apply STRIDE to each crossing. Spoofing threatens authentication, tampering threatens integrity, repudiation threatens accountability, information disclosure threatens confidentiality, denial of service threatens availability, and elevation of privilege threatens authorisation.

Rank threats roughly by likelihood and impact. A public, unauthenticated endpoint that touches payment data ranks above an internal report reachable only from a jump host. Precise scores matter less than agreeing on the top few.

For each high-ranked threat choose a response: mitigate (add a control), eliminate (remove the feature or data), transfer (use a provider that carries the risk) or accept it explicitly with an owner and a review date.

Turn mitigations into tickets and tests, and revisit the model when the design changes: a new integration, a new data store or a new kind of user. The model is a living document, not an approval gate.

useWhen: Use it when designing a new feature that handles sensitive data.
Use it when adding an integration that crosses an organisation boundary.
avoidWhen: Avoid modelling every minor UI change in full; reuse the existing model.
Avoid producing a document nobody revisits after launch.

rows: Code review with a security checklist
Missing features such as audit logs
Exploitable issues in the running system
Paths the testers were not told about

numbers.title: Is an hour of modelling worth it?
assumptions: A design flaw costs 2 engineer-days to fix on the whiteboard and 20 after launch (illustrative)
A one-hour session with 4 people finds one such flaw in half of features
steps: Session cost: 4 people × 1 hour = 4 engineer-hours, about half a day.
Expected saving per feature: 50% × (20 − 2) = 9 engineer-days.
Even if only 1 feature in 10 had such a flaw, the saving (1.8 days) still exceeds the half-day cost.
The numbers are illustrative; the point is the large gap between fixing designs and fixing shipped systems.
numbers.result: Short threat-modelling sessions pay for themselves when they catch even a small share of design flaws.

india.title: OWASP’s four-question framework
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet organises the practice around four questions: what are we working on, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, and did we do a good enough job. It recommends starting with a system model such as a data-flow diagram, using a structured method like STRIDE to identify threats, and treating the model as something revisited as the system changes rather than produced once.

pitfalls.trap: “We use HTTPS, so we are secure.”
pitfalls.say: “TLS protects data in transit; I’d still check who can call each endpoint and what they can reach.”

pitfalls.trap: “Threat modelling is for the security team.”
pitfalls.say: “The people who know the data flows are the engineers building them, so we run it ourselves and ask security to review.”

takeaways: Model data flows and trust boundaries first.
STRIDE gives six questions to ask at each boundary.
Rank threats and decide: mitigate, eliminate, transfer or accept.
Revisit the model when the design changes.

interactive.title: Which flow is the riskiest?
interactive.prompt: A service has: a public login endpoint, an internal metrics page on a private network, and a nightly job that copies the user table to an analytics bucket using a long-lived key stored in CI.

choices.label: The nightly copy with the long-lived CI key
choices.feedback: Right: a forgotten side path with broad data and a long-lived credential is a prime target.

choices.label: The internal metrics page
choices.feedback: It exposes little and is not reachable from outside.

choices.label: The login endpoint is the only real risk
choices.feedback: It matters, but it is usually the best-defended path.

interactive.reveal: List side paths (jobs, exports, CI) in your diagram; they often carry the most data with the least protection.

seeAlso.why: Authentication and authorisation are mitigations for spoofing and elevation
Untrusted input is what crosses trust boundaries

title: Hashing, MACs, Encryption and Signatures
objectives: Tell hashing, MACs, encryption and signatures apart by what they guarantee
Choose authenticated encryption for confidentiality
Avoid nonce reuse and home-made schemes

cards.title: Four tools, four guarantees
cards.body: A hash (SHA-256) fingerprints data: anyone can compute it, no key. A MAC (HMAC) proves data came from someone holding a shared key and was not altered. Encryption hides content from those without the key. A digital signature lets anyone with the public key verify that the private-key holder signed it.

cards.title: Symmetric and asymmetric keys
cards.body: Symmetric schemes (AES, HMAC) use one shared secret on both sides and are fast. Asymmetric schemes (RSA, elliptic-curve keys) use a public and a private key; they solve key distribution and signing but are slower, so protocols like TLS use them to agree on a symmetric key for the bulk data.

cards.title: Worked example: verifying a webhook
cards.body: A payment provider sends webhooks signed with HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body and a timestamp using a shared secret.
steps: Read the raw request body bytes before any JSON parsing changes them
Compute HMAC-SHA256(secret, timestamp + "." + body)
Compare with the signature header using a constant-time comparison
Reject if the timestamp is more than a few minutes old to block replays
Only then parse and act on the event

cards.title: Misconception: encryption proves who sent it
cards.body: Plain encryption without authentication can be altered undetectably: with some modes, flipping bits in the ciphertext flips the same bits in the plaintext. Use authenticated encryption (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305), which rejects any modified ciphertext.

cards.title: Trap: reusing a nonce
cards.body: AES-GCM needs a unique nonce for every message under the same key. Reusing one leaks the XOR of the two plaintexts and lets an attacker forge messages. Use a library that generates nonces for you, or rotate keys well before a counter could repeat.

questions.prompt: You need to detect tampering of messages between two services that share a secret. What fits?

choices.label: An HMAC over each message
A SHA-256 hash of each message
Encrypting each message with AES-CTR
A CRC-32 checksum on each message

questions.explanation: A plain hash or a CRC can be recomputed by an attacker after editing the message; a MAC needs the key. Unauthenticated CTR encryption hides content but is malleable, so flipped bits go undetected.

questions.prompt: Why does TLS use asymmetric keys only at the start?

choices.label: They are slow; a shared key is faster
They need a new certificate for each connection
Their keys must change for every record
They cannot provide forward secrecy

questions.explanation: Asymmetric operations are far slower, so the handshake uses them to agree a symmetric session key for bulk data. Ephemeral key exchange is what provides forward secrecy, the certificate is reused across many connections, and session keys do not change per record.

questions.prompt: Which mode both encrypts and detects modification?

choices.label: AES-GCM
AES-CTR without a MAC
AES-CBC without a MAC
AES-ECB

questions.explanation: GCM is authenticated encryption; the others need a separate MAC.

questions.prompt: Release files are published with a signature. What does checking it prove?

choices.label: The files are encrypted
The files were reviewed and contain no bugs
The key holder produced these bytes
The publisher’s server was not hacked

questions.explanation: A signature proves these bytes came unchanged from the key holder. It says nothing about quality or encryption. It catches files altered on a mirror or download server, but it cannot show the publisher was not hacked: an attacker who holds the signing key, or changes code before signing, produces a valid signature.

questions.prompt: Order safe webhook verification.

items.label: Read the raw body bytes
Compare in constant time
Compute the HMAC with the shared secret
Parse and process the event
Check the timestamp is recent

questions.explanation: Verify on raw bytes before trusting or parsing.

questions.prompt: You must encrypt customer documents at rest in your own service.

approaches.label: AES-CBC written from the spec by the team
A custom XOR scheme with a long key
A vetted library’s AEAD with keys from a key-management service

rationaleOptions.label: Implementing the spec carefully makes it safe
A long XOR key is as strong as AES
Key management handles storage and rotation
Authenticated encryption detects tampering

rationaleConflicts.r3: Repeating-key XOR is broken by frequency analysis.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Padding-oracle and timing flaws hide in correct-looking code.

questions.explanation: Use high-level, reviewed APIs; the hard parts are modes, nonces and keys.

flashcards.back: A hash needs no key; a MAC needs a shared key, so only key holders can produce it.
Integrity: modified ciphertext fails to decrypt.
Private key signs, public key verifies origin and integrity.

mechanism.title: What each primitive does and what it does not
steps: A cryptographic hash maps any input to a fixed-size digest. It is one-way and collision-resistant, but it is public: anyone can hash a modified message. Use it to fingerprint files or build other tools, not to prove who sent something.

A MAC such as HMAC mixes a secret key into the hash. Only holders of the key can compute a valid tag, so a matching tag proves integrity and origin among key holders. Compare tags in constant time, since an early-exit comparison leaks how many bytes matched.

Symmetric encryption hides content using a shared key. Modern practice is authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD): AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypts and produces a tag, and decryption fails if anything changed. Associated data, such as a record id, is authenticated but not encrypted.

Asymmetric cryptography uses key pairs. Encrypting to a public key lets anyone send secrets only the private-key holder can read; signing with a private key lets anyone verify with the public key. Key exchange (Diffie-Hellman) lets two parties derive a shared secret over an open channel.

Most failures are in usage, not algorithms: reused nonces, keys hard-coded in source, unauthenticated modes, or comparing secrets with ordinary string equality. High-level library APIs that pick modes and nonces remove most of these choices.

Keys need a lifecycle: generation from a secure random source, storage in a key-management service or hardware module, rotation, and revocation. Envelope encryption encrypts data with a data key and the data key with a master key, so rotating the master key does not require re-encrypting everything.

useWhen: Use AEAD for any data you encrypt yourself.
Use signatures when many parties must verify one publisher.
avoidWhen: Avoid inventing schemes or combining primitives by hand.
Avoid plain hashes where a key-holder check is needed.

rows: Integrity and origin among key holders
Integrity and origin anyone can verify

numbers.title: When does a random 96-bit nonce become risky?
assumptions: AES-GCM with random 96-bit nonces under one key
NIST guidance limits random-nonce GCM to 2^32 messages per key
steps: The chance of a repeated random nonce grows with the square of the message count (birthday bound).
At 2^32 (about 4.3 billion) messages the collision chance is about n² / 2^97 = 2^64 / 2^97 = 2^-33, inside the 2^-32 bound NIST sets.
A service encrypting 1,000 messages a second reaches 2^32 in 4.3 billion ÷ 1,000 ≈ 4.3 million seconds, about 50 days.
So rotate the key well before 50 days at that rate, or use a library that tracks usage.
numbers.result: High-volume encryption needs key rotation planned from message counts, not only from calendars.

india.title: NIST’s rules for GCM nonces
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: NIST Special Publication 800-38D defines Galois/Counter Mode and states that the probability that the authenticated encryption function is ever invoked with the same initialisation vector and the same key on two different sets of input data must be no greater than 2^-32. For randomly generated 96-bit IVs that means a single key should encrypt no more than 2^32 messages, which is why high-volume systems rotate keys or use deterministic counters.

pitfalls.trap: “We hash the token with SHA-256, so it cannot be forged.”
pitfalls.say: “Anyone can compute SHA-256; to prevent forgery I’d use an HMAC with a secret key or a signature.”

pitfalls.trap: “It’s encrypted, so it can’t be changed.”
pitfalls.say: “Only authenticated encryption detects changes; plain CBC or CTR can be bit-flipped.”

takeaways: Hash = fingerprint, MAC = shared-key proof, signature = public proof.
Use AEAD (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) for encryption.
Never reuse a nonce under the same key.
Use high-level libraries and a key-management service.

interactive.title: Is the webhook check safe?
interactive.prompt: A server verifies webhooks by parsing the JSON, re-serialising it, computing HMAC-SHA256 over that string and comparing with the header using ordinary string equality.

choices.label: No: it should hash the raw bytes and compare in constant time
choices.feedback: Right: re-serialising changes bytes, and early-exit comparison leaks timing.

choices.label: Yes: HMAC is secure, so the details do not matter
choices.feedback: The algorithm is fine; the usage around it is not.

choices.label: No: it should use MD5 instead
choices.feedback: MD5 is weaker; the issue is the raw body and comparison.

interactive.reveal: Verify the exact bytes received, compare tags in constant time, and reject stale timestamps.

title: Storing Passwords Safely
objectives: Explain why passwords need slow, salted hashes
Pick and tune Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2
Follow modern password-policy guidance

cards.title: Assume the database leaks
cards.body: Password storage is designed for the day an attacker copies the user table. The goal is that each stolen hash costs so much to crack that most passwords survive long enough for users to change them.

cards.title: Salts and work factors
cards.body: A unique random salt per password stops attackers cracking every account with one precomputed table and makes identical passwords hash differently. A work factor makes each guess deliberately slow and, for memory-hard functions, memory-hungry, which hurts GPU cracking rigs far more than one login on your server.

cards.title: Worked example: tuning bcrypt
cards.body: Choose a cost so one hash takes tens of milliseconds on your login servers.
steps: Benchmark: at cost 10 one hash takes about 60 ms on the production CPU (illustrative)
Each +1 doubles the work: cost 11 ≈ 120 ms, cost 12 ≈ 240 ms
Budget: login p99 must stay under 500 ms, and peak logins are 40 a second
Cost 11 uses 40 × 0.12 = 4.8 CPU-seconds per second, about 5 cores at peak
Store the cost with each hash so you can raise it later and rehash on next login

cards.title: Misconception: encrypting passwords is safer
cards.body: Encryption is reversible: whoever gets the key gets every password. Hashing is one-way; the server only needs to check a guess, never to recover the original. Store hashes, not ciphertext.

cards.title: Trap: fast hashes such as SHA-256
cards.body: General-purpose hashes are built to be fast, so a GPU can try billions of guesses a second against them. Salting does not slow each guess. Use a password-hashing function designed to be slow and tunable.

questions.prompt: Which is suited to storing passwords?

choices.label: SHA-256 with a unique salt
Argon2id with a unique salt
AES-256 with a server key
HMAC-SHA-256 with a secret pepper

questions.explanation: Password hashes must be slow and tunable; Argon2id is OWASP’s first choice. SHA-256 and HMAC are fast, so guesses stay cheap even with a salt or pepper, and AES is reversible by anyone with the key.

questions.prompt: Two users pick the same password. With per-user salts, what do their stored hashes look like?

choices.label: Identical, since the password is the same
Different from each other
Identical until one of them logs in again
Identical, but encrypted with different keys

questions.explanation: A unique salt per user makes identical passwords produce different hashes, so one cracked hash reveals nothing about the other. Hashes do not change on login, and password hashes are not encrypted.

questions.prompt: Raising bcrypt’s cost from 10 to 12 changes the time per hash by about how much?

choices.label: 12 times longer
2 times longer
20% longer
4 times longer

questions.explanation: The cost is a power of two: two steps is 2 × 2.

questions.prompt: An attacker’s rig tests 3,000 bcrypt guesses a second at your cost setting (illustrative). How many days to try a list of 1 billion common passwords against one stolen hash?
assumptions: One hash, one salt
Rate stays constant
questions.explanation: Design implication: a weak password on its own salt still falls in days, so slow hashing buys time; breach-list checks keep the weakest choices out.

questions.prompt: Order a safe login check.

items.label: Compare the result in constant time
Look up the user’s stored hash, salt and parameters
Hash the submitted password with those parameters
If parameters are outdated, rehash with the new ones and save

questions.explanation: Verify with stored settings, then upgrade.

questions.prompt: A legacy system stores unsalted SHA-1 password hashes and cannot force every user to reset.

approaches.label: Wrap each old hash in Argon2id now, then rehash plainly on next login
Keep SHA-1 until users log in again
Add a global salt to new hashes only

rationaleOptions.label: Waiting is fine because logins are frequent
Every stored hash becomes slow to crack immediately
Users who log in move to a clean Argon2id hash
Changing only new hashes protects old ones

rationaleConflicts.r3: Inactive accounts keep weak hashes for years.
rationaleConflicts.r4: The existing hashes stay crackable at full speed.

questions.explanation: Layering a slow hash over the old one upgrades everyone at once.

flashcards.back: To make identical passwords hash differently and defeat precomputed tables.
Argon2id (minimum 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, 1 parallelism).
Doubles the work per hash.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B: Authentication and Lifecycle Management

mechanism.title: How password hashing slows attackers
steps: On registration, generate a random salt, run the password-hashing function with chosen parameters, and store the algorithm, parameters, salt and output together, usually in one encoded string. On login, read those values and recompute.

Argon2id is memory-hard: each guess must fill and read a block of memory, so attackers cannot cheaply run thousands of guesses in parallel on a GPU. OWASP’s minimum recommendation is 19 MiB of memory, 2 iterations and parallelism 1; scrypt is a memory-hard alternative.

bcrypt uses a cost parameter where each +1 doubles the work; OWASP recommends at least 10. It reads at most 72 bytes of input, so very long passphrases are silently truncated unless you handle that. PBKDF2 is the choice when FIPS validation is required; OWASP suggests 600,000 iterations with HMAC-SHA-256.

A pepper is a secret added to every hash and kept outside the database, for example in a secrets manager. If only the database leaks, the attacker also needs the pepper. It complements salting; it does not replace it.

Parameters age as hardware improves. Store them with each hash; when a user logs in with outdated settings, rehash with current ones. For accounts that never log in, wrap the old hash in a new function.

Policy matters as much as hashing. NIST SP 800-63B advises checking new passwords against lists of breached and common passwords, allowing long passphrases, and not forcing periodic changes or composition rules, which push users to predictable patterns. The 2025 revision, SP 800-63B-4, makes this firmer: passwords used alone must be at least 15 characters (at least 8 when they are only one factor of MFA), and verifiers shall not impose composition rules or periodic changes, though they must force a change on evidence of compromise.

useWhen: Use Argon2id for new systems; bcrypt or scrypt where already in use.
Use rate limiting and breach-list checks alongside hashing.
avoidWhen: Avoid general-purpose hashes (SHA-*, MD5) for passwords.
Avoid encrypting passwords reversibly.

rows: Memory per login at high concurrency
Not memory-hard; GPUs are efficient against it

numbers.title: What one stolen hash costs to crack
assumptions: A cracking rig tries 3,000 guesses a second against one bcrypt hash at your cost (illustrative)
A fast SHA-256 hash on the same rig: about 10 billion guesses a second (illustrative)
steps: A list of the 1 billion most common passwords takes 1,000,000,000 ÷ 3,000 ≈ 333,333 s, about 3.9 days, per bcrypt hash.
With salts, each user must be attacked separately: for 1 million users that is about 10,600 years for the full list.
Against unsalted SHA-256, one pass over the list checks every user at once and takes about 0.1 s.
Raising bcrypt cost by 2 multiplies the attacker’s time by 4.
numbers.result: Salted slow hashes turn a mass breach into a per-user, per-guess cost; fast unsalted hashes fall in seconds.

india.title: OWASP’s recommended parameters
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet recommends Argon2id with a minimum of 19 MiB of memory, an iteration count of 2 and one degree of parallelism, falling back to scrypt, then bcrypt with a work factor of 10 or more and a 72-byte input limit, and PBKDF2 with 600,000 iterations of HMAC-SHA-256 where FIPS-140 compliance is required. It also describes upgrading legacy hashes by layering a modern algorithm over the old one.

pitfalls.trap: “We use SHA-256 with a salt, so passwords are safe.”
pitfalls.say: “Salt stops shared tables, but SHA-256 is fast; I’d move to Argon2id or bcrypt so each guess is expensive.”

pitfalls.trap: “Force a password change every 90 days.”
pitfalls.say: “NIST advises against forced periodic changes; I’d check against breached lists and change on evidence of compromise.”

takeaways: Store salted, slow, tunable hashes, never reversible ciphertext.
Argon2id first; bcrypt cost ≥ 10; PBKDF2 600,000 iterations if FIPS is needed.
Store parameters with each hash and upgrade on login.
Check new passwords against breach lists; skip forced rotation.

interactive.title: Tune the work factor
interactive.prompt: Your login server takes 60 ms per bcrypt hash at cost 10; an attacker’s rig tries 3,000 guesses a second at that cost (both illustrative). Slide the cost.
interactive.takeaway: Each step doubles both your cost per login and the attacker’s cost per guess. Pick the highest cost your login latency and peak CPU can afford, usually tens to a few hundred milliseconds.

Rate limiting slows online guessing

title: Tokens and JWTs Without the Pitfalls
objectives: Read the three parts of a JWT and what the signature covers
Validate algorithm, issuer, audience and expiry
Choose between self-contained tokens and server-side sessions

cards.title: A signed note, not a secret
cards.body: A JSON Web Token has a header, a payload of claims and a signature, each base64url-encoded and joined by dots. Anyone holding the token can decode and read the payload; the signature only proves the issuer created it and nobody changed it. Never put secrets in a JWT payload.

cards.title: Self-contained means hard to revoke
cards.body: A server can verify a JWT without a database lookup, which is why APIs like them. The flip side: a stolen token stays valid until it expires. Keep access tokens short-lived (minutes) and use refresh tokens, which the server can revoke, to get new ones.

cards.title: Worked example: validating an incoming token
cards.body: An API receives a bearer token from a known identity provider.
steps: Reject unless the header alg is on your allowlist, for example RS256 only
Fetch the issuer’s public key by key id from its published key set, cached
Verify the signature over header and payload
Check iss is the expected issuer and aud includes this API
Check exp is in the future and nbf has passed, allowing a small clock skew
Only then use sub and scope for authorisation

cards.title: Misconception: JWTs are more secure than session cookies
cards.body: They solve a different problem: verification without shared state. A session id in a cookie can be revoked instantly by deleting the server record; a JWT cannot. For a single web app with its own backend, plain server-side sessions are often simpler and safer.

cards.title: Trap: trusting the token’s own alg header
cards.body: Libraries that pick the verification algorithm from the token itself have accepted “alg”: “none” (no signature) or verified an RS256 token as HS256 using the public key as an HMAC secret. Configure the expected algorithm on the server and reject anything else.

questions.prompt: Who can read the claims in a signed (not encrypted) JWT?

choices.label: Anyone who holds the token
Only the issuing server
Only holders of the private key
Nobody once it is signed

questions.explanation: Signing protects integrity, not confidentiality; the payload is just base64url.

questions.prompt: A token arrives with header alg “none”. What should the API do?

choices.label: Reject it outright
Verify it with the HMAC key
Accept it if exp is valid
Log it and accept it

questions.explanation: The server, not the token, decides which algorithms are acceptable.

questions.prompt: A user’s 24-hour JWT is stolen. They click “log out of all devices”. What is the problem?

choices.label: The browser keeps it in its cache after logout
The server clears its session record only on the next request
The refresh token cannot be revoked before it expires
The token stays valid until it expires

questions.explanation: A self-contained token is checked by signature and expiry, not looked up, so there is no server session record to clear. Refresh tokens are stored by the server and can be revoked, but that does not stop an access token already issued. Use short lifetimes or a revocation check.

questions.prompt: Service A accepts tokens issued for Service B by the same provider. Which check is missing?

choices.label: Issued-at (iat)
Expiry (exp)
Subject (sub)
Audience (aud)

questions.explanation: aud says which API the token is for.

questions.prompt: Order the validation of an incoming JWT.

items.label: Check issuer, audience and expiry
Verify the signature
Look up the key by key id
Check alg against the allowlist
Authorise using subject and scopes

questions.explanation: Trust nothing in the token until the signature and claims check out.

questions.prompt: A single-page app and its own backend on one domain need logins that can be revoked at once by support staff.

approaches.label: Long-lived JWTs kept in localStorage
Server-side sessions with an HttpOnly, Secure cookie
JWTs with a 30-day expiry and no refresh

rationaleOptions.label: Deleting the session record revokes access instantly
JWTs avoid all database lookups so they are better here
HttpOnly cookies are not readable by injected scripts
localStorage is as safe as an HttpOnly cookie

rationaleConflicts.r3: With one backend, a session lookup is cheap and buys instant revocation.

questions.explanation: Pick tokens for multi-service verification; pick sessions when revocation and simplicity matter.

flashcards.back: Header, payload, signature; base64url, dot-separated.
Allowed alg, signature, iss, aud, exp/nbf.
A stolen JWT works until it expires.

mechanism.title: How token-based authentication works end to end
steps: An identity provider authenticates the user and issues a token signed with its private key (RS256, ES256) or a shared secret (HS256). The token carries claims: iss (issuer), sub (subject), aud (audience), exp (expiry), and often scopes or roles.

The client sends the token in an Authorization: Bearer header. Any service with the issuer’s public key can verify it locally, which avoids a central session lookup on every call and suits many services behind one identity provider.

The issuer publishes its public keys as a JSON Web Key Set at a well-known URL. Tokens name the key by kid, which lets the issuer rotate keys: publish the new key, start signing with it, and remove the old one after the longest token lifetime.

Validation must be strict. RFC 8725 recommends that libraries let callers specify the allowed algorithms and that applications check issuer and audience. Accepting whatever alg the header names has led to repeated vulnerabilities.

Revocation is the weak spot. Common answers: short access tokens (5–15 minutes) with revocable refresh tokens, a deny-list of token ids checked for high-risk actions, or opaque tokens checked by introspection. Each adds back some of the state JWTs avoided.

Storage in the browser matters. Tokens in localStorage are readable by any script on the page, so an XSS bug can steal them; HttpOnly cookies cannot be read by scripts but need CSRF protection. Many teams keep tokens on a backend and give the browser a session cookie.

useWhen: Use JWTs when many services must verify identity without a shared session store.
Use short lifetimes plus refresh tokens for revocation.
avoidWhen: Avoid JWTs as a session replacement for one simple web app.
Avoid storing sensitive data in the payload.

numbers.title: How long a stolen token stays useful
assumptions: Access token lifetime 10 minutes, refresh token revocable (illustrative)
Detection of a stolen session takes 30 minutes
steps: With a 24-hour JWT and no revocation, an attacker keeps access for up to 24 hours whatever you do.
With 10-minute access tokens, revoking the refresh token at minute 30 ends access by minute 40 at most.
Exposure shrinks from 24 hours to about 40 minutes, a 36× reduction.
The cost: a refresh call every 10 minutes per active client.
numbers.result: Short access tokens bound the damage of theft to detection time plus one token lifetime.

india.title: What the JWT best-practice RFC asks for
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 8725, the IETF’s JSON Web Token Best Current Practices, describes attacks seen in real deployments, including tokens with alg “none” being accepted and RSA public keys being misused as HMAC secrets. It requires that libraries let the application specify which algorithms are acceptable, that applications validate the issuer and audience, and recommends explicit typing so a token of one kind cannot be substituted for another.

pitfalls.trap: “It’s a JWT, so the data is encrypted.”
pitfalls.say: “A signed JWT is readable by anyone; I’d keep secrets out of it or use encrypted tokens.”

pitfalls.trap: “We’ll revoke tokens on logout.”
pitfalls.say: “A JWT can’t be revoked by itself; I’d keep access tokens short and revoke the refresh token.”

takeaways: A JWT is signed, not hidden: anyone can read it.
Pin the algorithm; check iss, aud, exp.
Short access tokens plus revocable refresh tokens.
For one web app, server sessions are often simpler.

interactive.title: Is the token accepted?
interactive.prompt: An API is configured to verify RS256 tokens. An attacker takes a valid token, changes the role claim to “admin”, sets alg to “none” and removes the signature. The library honours the alg header.

choices.label: Yes: the vulnerable library skips verification and the forged admin token works
choices.feedback: Right: trusting the token’s alg header is the bug.

choices.label: No: the role claim cannot be edited
choices.feedback: Base64url is easy to edit; only the signature stops changes.

choices.label: No: TLS would block it
choices.feedback: TLS protects transport, not the token’s contents.

interactive.reveal: Fix: configure the allowed algorithms on the server and reject tokens that do not match.

title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
objectives: Tell delegated authorisation (OAuth) from login (OpenID Connect)
Walk the authorisation code flow with PKCE
Validate redirect URIs, state and scopes

cards.title: OAuth delegates access; it does not log anyone in
cards.body: OAuth 2.0 lets a user grant an app limited access to their data at another service, such as “read my calendar”, without sharing their password. The app receives an access token for that API. OpenID Connect adds an ID token on top, which tells the app who the user is.

cards.title: Roles in the flow
cards.body: The resource owner (user) approves; the client (your app) requests; the authorisation server authenticates the user and issues tokens; the resource server (API) accepts access tokens. Keeping these roles straight explains most of the flow.

cards.title: Worked example: authorisation code flow with PKCE
cards.body: A web or mobile app signs a user in with an external identity provider.
steps: App generates a random code_verifier and sends its SHA-256 hash as code_challenge, plus a random state, to the authorisation endpoint
User logs in at the provider and approves the requested scopes
Provider redirects to the registered redirect URI with a short-lived code and the state
App checks state matches, then exchanges the code plus code_verifier at the token endpoint
Provider checks the verifier matches the challenge and returns access, refresh and ID tokens

cards.title: Misconception: an access token proves who the user is
cards.body: An access token is meant for an API; your app should not treat it as proof of identity, because a token issued to another app could be replayed to yours. Use the ID token, validated with your client id as its audience, for login.

cards.title: Trap: loose redirect URI matching
cards.body: If the provider accepts any redirect URI that starts with your domain, or allows wildcards, an attacker can steer the code to a page they control. Register exact redirect URIs and keep them exact.

questions.prompt: Which token tells your app who signed in?

choices.label: The authorisation code
The access token
The ID token
The refresh token

questions.explanation: OpenID Connect’s ID token is addressed to your app and carries the user’s identity.

questions.prompt: What does PKCE protect against?

choices.label: Users choosing weak passwords
Slow responses from the token endpoint
A stolen authorisation code being redeemed
Expired certificates at the provider

questions.explanation: Only the app that created the verifier can redeem the code.

questions.prompt: Why does the app send and check a random state value?

choices.label: To encrypt the access token on its way back
To prove the client’s identity to the token endpoint
To stop the code being redeemed twice
To tie the response to its own request

questions.explanation: state ties the redirect to a request this browser started, defending against cross-site request forgery on the callback. Client authentication and PKCE prove who redeems the code, and the authorisation server enforces single use.

questions.prompt: Which flow does current OAuth security guidance advise against?

choices.label: Refresh token rotation
Authorisation code with PKCE
Client credentials
The implicit flow

questions.explanation: RFC 9700 says the implicit grant should not be used; tokens leak via URLs.

questions.prompt: Order the authorisation code flow with PKCE.

items.label: User logs in and approves scopes
App sends code_challenge and state to the provider
App exchanges code and code_verifier for tokens
Provider redirects back with code and state

questions.explanation: Challenge, approve, redirect, exchange.

questions.prompt: A backend batch job needs to call a partner API on its own behalf, with no user involved.

approaches.label: Authorisation code flow with a service account’s password
Reuse an engineer’s personal refresh token
Client credentials grant with a narrowly scoped client

rationaleOptions.label: A person’s token works and is simpler
Scopes can be limited to what the job needs
The code flow suits jobs if you script the login
The job authenticates as itself, not as a person

rationaleConflicts.r3: It breaks when they leave and grants their full access.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Scripting a user login defeats its purpose and stores a password.

questions.explanation: Use client credentials for machine-to-machine calls.

flashcards.back: OAuth grants API access; OIDC adds an ID token for login.
A verifier/challenge pair so only the requesting app can redeem the code.
Register and match them exactly.

sources.title: RFC 7636: Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE)
RFC 9700: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security

mechanism.title: Why the flow has so many steps
steps: The browser is an untrusted channel: URLs land in history, logs and referrer headers. So the provider sends only a short-lived, single-use code through the browser, and the tokens travel over a direct back-channel request from the app to the token endpoint.

Confidential clients (server-side apps) authenticate to the token endpoint with a client secret. Public clients (mobile and single-page apps) cannot keep secrets, so PKCE replaces the secret: the code is useless without the verifier only the original app holds. RFC 9700 recommends PKCE for all clients.
Scopes limit what an access token can do, such as read-only calendar access. Ask for the fewest scopes needed; users see them on the consent screen and APIs enforce them.

OpenID Connect standardises login on top: request the openid scope and receive an ID token, a JWT whose audience is your client id, with the user’s subject identifier and an optional nonce you sent to prevent replay.

Refresh tokens let the app get new access tokens without the user. For public clients, providers rotate them: each use returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, so a stolen copy is detected when both parties try to use it.

Common mistakes: accepting access tokens as login proof, skipping state or nonce checks, wildcard redirect URIs, and keeping the deprecated implicit or password grants. Most libraries handle the flow correctly if configured with exact URIs and PKCE.

useWhen: Use OIDC with the code flow and PKCE for “Sign in with …”.
Use client credentials for service-to-service calls.
avoidWhen: Avoid the implicit and resource-owner password grants.
Avoid treating any access token as proof of identity.

numbers.title: Why the code must be short-lived
assumptions: Codes expire after 60 seconds and are single-use (illustrative; RFC 6749 recommends a maximum of 10 minutes)
A code leaks through a log that an attacker reads every 5 minutes
steps: With a 10-minute code lifetime, a log read within 10 minutes may find a usable code.
With 60 seconds and single use, the app has normally redeemed the code within a second, so the copy is already spent.
With PKCE, even an unspent code fails without the verifier.
Short lifetime, single use and PKCE stack: each blocks a different timing of the leak.
numbers.result: Codes in URLs leak; keep them short-lived, single-use and bound to the client with PKCE.

india.title: The 2025 OAuth security best practice
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 9700, the IETF’s Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security published in January 2025, records attacks seen against real deployments and updates the original framework. It says clients should use PKCE, the implicit grant should not be used, the resource owner password credentials grant must not be used, and authorisation servers must compare redirect URIs exactly against those registered, apart from port numbers for local loopback addresses.

pitfalls.trap: “We use OAuth for login.”
pitfalls.say: “OAuth grants API access; for login I’d use OpenID Connect and validate the ID token’s audience.”

pitfalls.trap: “PKCE is only for mobile apps.”
pitfalls.say: “Current guidance recommends PKCE for all clients, including server-side ones.”

takeaways: OAuth delegates API access; OIDC adds identity.
Use the code flow with PKCE for every client.
Exact redirect URIs, checked state and nonce.
Implicit and password grants are deprecated.

interactive.title: Can the attacker log in?
interactive.prompt: A malicious app on the same phone registers the same custom URL scheme and intercepts the redirect carrying the authorisation code. The legitimate app used PKCE.

choices.label: No: the code cannot be exchanged without the code_verifier
choices.feedback: Right: that is exactly the attack PKCE was designed for.

choices.label: Yes: the code alone is enough to get tokens
choices.feedback: It would be without PKCE.

choices.label: Yes, if the attacker also knows the client id
choices.feedback: Client ids are public; the verifier is the secret.

interactive.reveal: PKCE binds the code to the app instance that started the flow.

title: Broken Access Control
objectives: Spot insecure direct object references and missing function-level checks
Enforce authorisation on the server for every object
Apply least privilege and deny by default

cards.title: The most common serious flaw
cards.body: OWASP ranked broken access control first in its 2021 Top 10, where 94% of the applications were tested for some form of it, and kept it first in the 2025 edition. The pattern is simple: the app checks that you are logged in, but not that this record, action or tenant belongs to you.

cards.title: Object-level checks
cards.body: An insecure direct object reference (IDOR) happens when a request names an object by id, such as GET /invoices/1043, and the server returns it without checking ownership. Changing 1043 to 1044 shows someone else’s invoice. Every lookup must be scoped to what the caller may see.

cards.title: Worked example: fixing an invoice endpoint
cards.body: GET /invoices/{id} returns any invoice to any logged-in user.
steps: Identify the caller from the session or token, not from a request parameter
Query by both id and owner: WHERE id = :id AND account_id = :caller_account
Return 404 when nothing matches, so outsiders cannot tell which ids exist
Put the scoping in one shared data-access function rather than each handler
Add a test where user A requests user B’s invoice and expects 404

cards.title: Misconception: random ids fix it
cards.body: Unguessable ids (UUIDs) make enumeration harder, but ids leak through URLs, logs, shared links and browser history. They are a speed bump, not an access check. The server still has to verify the caller may access the object.

cards.title: Trap: hiding the button instead of checking the action
cards.body: Removing the “Delete user” button for non-admins does nothing if the DELETE endpoint does not check the role. Attackers call APIs directly. Enforce every permission on the server; the UI only reflects it.

questions.prompt: A user changes /orders/500 to /orders/501 and sees a stranger’s order. What is missing?

choices.label: TLS on the order endpoint
Input length validation
A larger order id space
An ownership check on the order

questions.explanation: The server must check the caller may access that object.

questions.prompt: Where must the “admins only” rule for deleting users be enforced?

choices.label: In the admin page’s frontend route guard
In the client app’s role check before the call
In the server handler for the delete
By hiding the delete button from non-admins

questions.explanation: Route guards, client-side role checks and hidden buttons all run on the client, which an attacker controls; anyone can call the endpoint directly. Only the server handler sees every request.

questions.prompt: A reporting service needs to read two tables. What database access should it get?

choices.label: Full admin so permission errors cannot cause outages
Read-only access to those two tables
The same login as the main app
Write access to all tables

questions.explanation: Least privilege limits damage if the service is compromised.

questions.prompt: For a record the caller may not see, which response leaks least?

choices.label: 500 with a stack trace
404 Not Found
403 with the owner’s name
200 with an empty body

questions.explanation: A uniform 404 hides whether the id exists.

questions.prompt: Order a safe object lookup.

items.label: Perform the action and log it
Load the object scoped to the caller’s tenant
Check the caller’s role allows this action
Authenticate the caller

questions.explanation: Identify, scope, authorise, act.

questions.prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS has 200 endpoints, each written by different engineers, and recently had a cross-tenant data leak.

approaches.label: Enforce tenant scoping in a shared data-access layer, with tests per endpoint
Ask each engineer to re-check their endpoints
Switch all ids to UUIDs

rationaleOptions.label: Careful engineers make central enforcement unnecessary
Tests catch new endpoints that bypass it
A single place to get scoping right
Unguessable ids stop cross-tenant access

rationaleConflicts.r3: The leak shows per-endpoint checks get missed.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Ids leak; the server still needs a check.

questions.explanation: Make the safe path the default path, then test it.

flashcards.back: Accessing an object by changing its id because the server skips the ownership check.
Access is refused unless a rule explicitly grants it.
Each user or service gets only the access it needs.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 2021: A01 Broken Access Control
OWASP: Insecure Direct Object Reference Prevention
CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP Top 10:2025: A01 Broken Access Control

mechanism.title: Designing authorisation that is hard to forget
steps: Authentication answers who is calling; authorisation answers whether they may do this to this object. Most broken access control is a missing second question, usually because a handler trusts that being logged in is enough.

Deny by default: an endpoint or object is inaccessible unless a rule grants access. Frameworks that require each route to declare its policy, and fail closed when none is declared, turn forgotten checks into visible errors.

Check at the object level, not only the route level. A role may allow “view invoices”, but each invoice must still belong to the caller’s account. Scoping queries by tenant or owner in a shared data-access layer makes the check hard to skip.

Models: role-based access control (RBAC) maps roles to permissions; attribute-based (ABAC) evaluates rules over user, resource and context attributes; relationship-based models (as in Google’s Zanzibar paper) derive access from graphs such as “member of folder”.
Least privilege applies to services too: database users, cloud roles and API keys should carry only the permissions their job needs, so a compromised component cannot reach everything.

Test authorisation explicitly: for each endpoint, a test where a user from another tenant or with a lower role tries the action and must fail. Log denials; a burst of 403s or 404s from one account often means someone is probing ids.

useWhen: Use central policy checks and tenant-scoped queries for every data access path.
Use cross-tenant and lower-role tests for each new endpoint, run in CI.
Use audit logs of denied requests to spot id probing early.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on hidden UI or unguessable ids.
Avoid shared, all-powerful service credentials.

rows: Access to the wrong tenant’s objects

numbers.title: How fast an unchecked id is enumerated
assumptions: Sequential order ids, about 2 million issued (illustrative)
Attacker sends 50 requests a second from one account
steps: Fetching all 2,000,000 ids takes 2,000,000 ÷ 50 = 40,000 s, about 11 hours.
Spread over 10 accounts or addresses it takes about 1.1 hours.
Rate limits slow this, but every fetched record is still a breach.
An ownership check returns 404 for all but the attacker’s own orders, so the scan yields nothing.
numbers.result: Rate limits and random ids slow enumeration; only the authorisation check stops it.

india.title: Broken access control in the OWASP Top 10
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The 2021 OWASP Top 10 moved broken access control to the first position. OWASP reports that 94% of applications were tested for some form of it and lists common weaknesses including violating least privilege or deny by default, bypassing checks by modifying the URL or parameters, permitting viewing or editing of someone else’s account by its identifier, and accessing APIs with missing access controls for POST, PUT and DELETE.

pitfalls.trap: “The ids are UUIDs, so nobody can guess them.”
pitfalls.say: “Ids leak through links and logs; I’d still check ownership on every request.”

pitfalls.trap: “Only admins see that page.”
pitfalls.say: “The page is hidden, but I’d check the role in the API handler, since anyone can call it.”

takeaways: Check ownership on every object access, server-side.
Deny by default; make policy declarations mandatory.
Scope queries by tenant in one shared layer.
Grant services least privilege.

interactive.title: What does the attacker get?
interactive.prompt: GET /api/accounts/{id}/statements checks that the caller is logged in. A logged-in attacker requests ids 1 to 1,000.

choices.label: Statements for every existing account in that range
choices.feedback: Right: authentication without object-level authorisation is an IDOR.

choices.label: Only their own statements
choices.feedback: That needs an ownership check the endpoint lacks.

choices.label: Nothing: logging in prevents this
choices.feedback: Being logged in says nothing about which accounts are yours.

interactive.reveal: Scope the lookup by the caller’s account and return 404 otherwise.

title: Managing Secrets
objectives: Keep secrets out of source code, images and logs
Deliver secrets at runtime from a secrets manager
Rotate secrets and respond to a leak

cards.title: What counts as a secret
cards.body: Anything that grants access: database passwords, API keys, signing keys, cloud credentials, webhook secrets, private TLS keys. If someone who reads it can act as your system, it is a secret and needs the same care as a password.

cards.title: Out of the repository
cards.body: Source code is copied widely: laptops, CI caches, forks, backups, contractors. A secret committed once stays in the history even after deletion. Configuration that varies per environment belongs outside the code; secrets belong in a dedicated secrets manager.

cards.title: Worked example: responding to a leaked key
cards.body: A cloud access key is found in a public repository commit from an hour ago.
steps: Revoke or disable the key immediately; deleting the commit is not enough
Issue a new key through the secrets manager and redeploy consumers
Search cloud audit logs for actions taken with the old key since the commit
Remove the secret from history if needed, and add a pre-commit secret scanner
Write up how it got there and what would have caught it earlier

cards.title: Misconception: private repositories are safe for secrets
cards.body: Private repositories are read by every employee with access, by CI systems and by any tool granted read access. Access lists drift, and a leaked laptop or token exposes everything in them. Treat repository access as wide, not secret.

cards.title: Trap: secrets in logs and error pages
cards.body: Request logging that records headers captures Authorization tokens; debug pages print environment variables; crash reports include configuration. Redact known secret fields at the logger and keep debug output off in production.

questions.prompt: An API key was pushed to a public repository. What is the first step?

choices.label: Rewrite the Git history to remove it
Make the repository private
Revoke the key
Rotate it at the next scheduled rotation

questions.explanation: Assume it was copied within minutes, because scanners watch public repositories. Only revocation stops its use. History rewrites come afterwards, and waiting for scheduled rotation leaves it live.

questions.prompt: Where should a production database password live?

choices.label: In a secrets manager, read at runtime
In the Git repository
Baked into the container image at build time
In an environment file on each server

questions.explanation: A secrets manager keeps it out of code and images, adds access control and audit, and allows rotation. Repositories, image layers and files on each server are copied, backed up and hard to rotate.

questions.prompt: Why prefer short-lived credentials issued per workload?

choices.label: A leaked one expires on its own
They remove the need for a secrets manager
They can be shared between workloads safely
Logging systems cannot record them by accident

questions.explanation: Short lifetimes bound the damage of a leak. They are usually issued by a secrets manager or identity service, and each workload should get its own so access can be scoped and traced.

questions.prompt: A container image build copies a .env file with keys, then deletes it in a later step. Is the secret gone?

choices.label: No, but only the build machine still has it
Yes, deleted files are removed
No, it remains in an earlier layer
Yes, if the image is private

questions.explanation: Image layers are additive: anyone who pulls the image can extract the earlier layer, private or not. Use build-time secret mounts that never enter a layer.

questions.prompt: Order a zero-downtime secret rotation.

items.label: Switch all clients to the new secret
Create the new secret alongside the old
Configure consumers to accept or use the new one
Revoke the old secret

questions.explanation: Overlap, switch, then retire.

questions.prompt: Services on a cloud platform need database credentials.

approaches.label: Credentials committed to a private repository
One shared password in an environment file on each server
Workload identity fetching short-lived credentials from a secrets manager

rationaleOptions.label: Rotation needs no redeploy of code
Each service has its own audited identity
A shared password is easier to rotate
Private repositories are access-controlled enough

rationaleConflicts.r3: Changing it means updating every server at once.
rationaleConflicts.r4: History keeps old secrets and access spreads widely.

questions.explanation: Identity-based, short-lived credentials make rotation routine.

flashcards.front: Secret committed by mistake: first action?
flashcards.back: Revoke it; then rotate, check logs, clean history.
Run old and new in parallel, switch, then revoke.
Store config in the environment, separate from code.

mechanism.title: From hard-coded keys to short-lived credentials
steps: Level 0 is a secret in source code. Level 1 moves it to environment variables or config files outside the repository. Level 2 stores it in a secrets manager that encrypts it, controls who can read it and logs each access.

Level 3 removes long-lived secrets: workloads prove their identity to the platform (a cloud role, a Kubernetes service account) and receive short-lived credentials. Dynamic secrets go further, with the secrets manager creating a unique database user per service that expires automatically.

Delivery: applications read secrets at start-up or on demand from the manager’s API, or the platform mounts them as files. Environment variables are simple but are inherited by child processes and often dumped in crash reports, so files or API reads are safer for high-value secrets.

Rotation needs overlap. Systems that accept two valid secrets at once (two API keys, two signing keys by key id) can rotate without downtime: add new, move clients, remove old. Systems with only one slot force a coordinated cut-over.

Detection: scan commits before they are pushed and scan repositories continuously; many providers also scan public code for their key formats and revoke or notify. Treat any alert as a leak until proven otherwise.
Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted, by default; enable encryption at rest for etcd and restrict who can read Secret objects, or sync from an external manager.

useWhen: Use a secrets manager and workload identity in production.
Use pre-commit scanning in every repository.
avoidWhen: Avoid secrets in code, images, tickets or chat.
Avoid long-lived keys shared across services.

rows: Anyone with server or backup access

numbers.title: How long does a leaked key stay useful?
assumptions: Static key, rotated yearly; leak detected after 30 days (illustrative)
Alternative: credentials valid for 1 hour, renewed automatically
steps: Static key: the attacker keeps access until someone notices and revokes: 30 days here, up to a year if nobody notices.
Short-lived credential: a copy stops working within 1 hour, even if nobody notices.
30 days is 720 hours, so exposure shrinks about 720 times.
The attacker would need ongoing access to the workload to keep minting new credentials, which is easier to detect.
numbers.result: Short-lived credentials turn an undetected leak from months of access into at most an hour.

india.title: A repository full of keys
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: Publicly reported in the US Federal Trade Commission’s complaint against Uber: in 2016 attackers used an access key that an Uber engineer had posted in a private code repository to download data on about 57 million riders and drivers from cloud storage. The key gave broad access and was long-lived. The case is often cited for two lessons: private repositories are not a safe place for secrets, and broad, long-lived credentials magnify any leak.

pitfalls.trap: “We deleted the commit, so the key is safe.”
pitfalls.say: “Anyone could have cloned it already; I’d revoke and rotate the key first.”

pitfalls.trap: “Kubernetes Secrets are encrypted.”
pitfalls.say: “By default they are only base64-encoded; I’d enable encryption at rest and limit read access.”

takeaways: Secrets belong in a secrets manager, not code or images.
Prefer short-lived, identity-based credentials.
Rotate with overlap: add new, switch, revoke old.
On a leak, revoke first, investigate second.

interactive.title: Is the secret still exposed?
interactive.prompt: A developer commits a database password, notices five minutes later, and pushes a new commit that removes it. The repository is public.

choices.label: Yes: it is in history and may already be copied; rotate it
choices.feedback: Right: removal does not undo exposure.

choices.label: No: the latest commit no longer contains it
choices.feedback: History still contains it and automated scrapers watch public pushes.

choices.label: Only if someone forked the repository
choices.feedback: Cloning, caching and scraping do not need a fork.

interactive.reveal: Rotate the password, then check the database logs for unknown connections.

title: Server-Side Request Forgery
objectives: Recognise features that make the server fetch user-supplied URLs
Explain why internal addresses and metadata services are the prize
Defend with allowlists, network egress rules and safer metadata access

cards.title: Your server makes the request
cards.body: Server-side request forgery (SSRF) happens when an attacker gets your server to fetch a URL of their choosing: a link preview, a webhook target, an image import. The request comes from inside your network, so it can reach admin panels, internal APIs and cloud metadata services the attacker cannot reach directly.

cards.title: The cloud metadata prize
cards.body: Cloud virtual machines can query a link-local address (169.254.169.254) for information about themselves, including temporary credentials for the machine’s role. An SSRF that can read that address can hand those credentials to the attacker.

cards.title: Worked example: hardening a link-preview fetcher
cards.body: Users paste a URL and the server fetches it to show a title and image.
steps: Allow only http and https schemes
Resolve the host name, then reject private, loopback, link-local and metadata addresses
Connect to the address you checked, not a fresh lookup, to block DNS rebinding
Disable redirects, or re-check every redirect target the same way
Run the fetcher in a network zone whose egress firewall blocks internal ranges

cards.title: Misconception: a deny-list of “localhost” is enough
cards.body: Addresses have many spellings: 127.1, 0x7f000001, [::1], a DNS name that resolves to 10.0.0.5, or a redirect from an allowed site. String checks on the URL miss them. Check the resolved address, and back it with network controls.

cards.title: Trap: returning the fetched body to the user
cards.body: If the response is shown to the attacker, SSRF becomes a read primitive for internal services. Return only what the feature needs (a title, a thumbnail) and cap size and time, so even a mistaken fetch leaks little.

questions.prompt: Which feature is most exposed to SSRF?

choices.label: Resizing an image already stored
Accepting an uploaded image file
Showing a static logo on the page
Importing an image from a user-given URL

questions.explanation: Only the URL import makes the server fetch an attacker-chosen address.

questions.prompt: Why is 169.254.169.254 a common SSRF target?

choices.label: It can hand out the machine’s cloud credentials
It is the default gateway for traffic leaving the machine
It hosts the public website
It stores user passwords

questions.explanation: Instance metadata services expose role credentials to the machine.

questions.prompt: A URL check passes for files.example.com, which then redirects to http://10.0.0.5/admin. What went wrong?

choices.label: The DNS name resolved to a public address
TLS was not verified
Redirect targets were not re-checked
The request used https instead of http

questions.explanation: The first host passed, but the redirect led to an internal address that was never checked. Each hop must pass the same checks, or redirects bypass them. The first name resolving to a public address is why the check passed, and the scheme or TLS of the first hop does not change where the redirect goes.

questions.prompt: How does AWS IMDSv2 make SSRF theft harder?

choices.label: It removes credentials from the metadata service
It requires a session token obtained via PUT
It only answers requests made over HTTPS
It encrypts the credentials it returns

questions.explanation: IMDSv2 requires a session token fetched with a PUT and a custom header, which a simple GET-only SSRF cannot send. It still answers over plain HTTP on the link-local address and returns credentials unencrypted to callers that complete the flow.

questions.prompt: Order the checks before fetching a user-supplied URL.

items.label: Resolve the host name to an address
Reject private and link-local addresses
Connect to that same checked address
Check the scheme is http or https

questions.explanation: Validate what you will actually connect to.

questions.prompt: A webhook feature lets customers register any HTTPS URL to receive events.
constraints: Servers run in a cloud VPC

approaches.label: Trust customers to enter valid URLs
Send webhooks from an isolated egress service that blocks internal ranges
Check URLs against a list of banned host names

rationaleOptions.label: Network rules hold even if URL parsing is fooled
Banning “localhost” and “internal” names covers it
Customers are authenticated, so URLs are safe
A compromise of the sender reaches nothing internal

rationaleConflicts.r3: Numeric, encoded and DNS-based spellings bypass name lists.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Any customer account can be an attacker’s.

questions.explanation: Layer address checks with network isolation for URL-fetching features.

flashcards.back: Making the server send requests to attacker-chosen destinations.
The instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254.

mechanism.title: Why SSRF is hard to block with input checks alone
steps: URL parsers disagree. One library may read http://a.com@10.0.0.5/ as host a.com and another as 10.0.0.5. Validate with the same parsed result you will use to connect, and prefer allowlists of known hosts where the feature permits.

DNS can change between check and use. In a DNS rebinding attack, a name resolves to a public address during validation and to an internal one when the request is made. Resolve once, validate the address, and connect to that exact address.

Redirects and alternative schemes widen the hole: a permitted site redirects to an internal address, or a file:// or gopher:// URL reaches local files or other protocols. Disable redirects or re-validate each, and allow only the schemes the feature needs.

Cloud metadata services are the usual goal. AWS IMDSv2 requires a PUT request to obtain a session token and sets a low hop limit on the response, which defeats most simple SSRF; other clouds require a special request header. Enforce the newer version on every instance.

Network controls catch what code misses: run URL-fetching components in a subnet whose egress rules deny private ranges and the metadata address, or route them through a proxy that enforces the policy.
Limit what a successful SSRF can do: give instance roles least privilege, keep internal services authenticated rather than trusting “inside the network”, and return minimal data from fetches.

useWhen: Use isolated, egress-restricted fetchers for user URLs.
Use IMDSv2 or the equivalent hardened metadata access.
avoidWhen: Avoid string-based deny-lists as the only control.
Avoid unauthenticated internal admin endpoints.

rows: SSRF that can send PUT with headers

numbers.title: How broad a stolen role credential is
assumptions: A web server role can read every object bucket in the account (illustrative)
Temporary credentials from metadata typically stay valid for several hours
steps: One SSRF read of the metadata endpoint yields credentials valid for hours.
With broad storage permissions, the attacker can list and download every bucket in that time.
With a least-privilege role (one bucket, read-only, one prefix), the same theft exposes one prefix.
The SSRF bug is the same; the blast radius differs by the role’s permissions.
numbers.result: SSRF severity is set by what the server’s identity can reach; least privilege caps it.

india.title: A firewall that fetched credentials
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: Publicly reported in Capital One’s 2019 disclosure and the related US court filings: an attacker exploited a misconfigured web application firewall to make requests from inside Capital One’s cloud environment, obtained credentials for a role with broad storage access, and copied data on about 100 million people in the US and about 6 million in Canada. It became a standard example of SSRF reaching an instance metadata service, and one reason cloud providers pushed hardened metadata access. In the OWASP Top 10:2025, SSRF no longer has its own entry; it is folded into A01 Broken Access Control.

pitfalls.trap: “We block requests to localhost.”
pitfalls.say: “Internal addresses have many spellings and DNS can point anywhere; I’d check the resolved address and restrict egress.”

pitfalls.trap: “It’s only an internal endpoint.”
pitfalls.say: “SSRF turns any server into an internal client, so internal services still need authentication.”

takeaways: SSRF turns your server into the attacker’s proxy.
Validate the resolved address you connect to; handle redirects.
Restrict egress and harden metadata access (IMDSv2).
Least privilege on server roles limits the damage.

title: Software Supply Chain Security
objectives: Name the ways dependencies and build systems get compromised
Pin, verify and inventory what you ship
Explain provenance and the SLSA levels at a high level

cards.title: You ship code you did not write
cards.body: A typical service pulls in hundreds of open-source packages, base images and build tools. Each one, and each maintainer account and build server behind it, can introduce malicious code into your product. Supply-chain security is about knowing what you ship and trusting how it was built.

cards.title: Common attack paths
cards.body: Typosquatting (a package named like a popular one), dependency confusion (a public package with the same name as your internal one), a hijacked maintainer account, a compromised build server, or a long-trusted maintainer who turns malicious. Each injects code that runs with your service’s permissions.

cards.title: Worked example: tightening a dependency pipeline
cards.body: A team wants confidence that what runs in production matches what was reviewed.
steps: Commit a lockfile so every build resolves the same versions and hashes
Configure package managers to use your internal registry or scoped names, closing dependency confusion
Build in CI only, from a clean environment, and record build provenance
Sign images and verify signatures at deploy time
Generate an SBOM per release and scan it for known vulnerabilities

cards.title: Misconception: popular packages are safe
cards.body: Popularity attracts attackers: compromising one widely used package reaches thousands of downstream projects. Popular projects are better reviewed on average, but a maintainer account takeover or a malicious release can still slip through, so pin and verify regardless.

cards.title: Trap: install scripts run with your permissions
cards.body: Many package managers run scripts during installation. A malicious dependency can read environment variables, CI secrets and SSH keys the moment it is installed, before any test runs. Restrict install scripts where possible and keep secrets out of build steps that install third-party code.

questions.prompt: An internal package “acme-utils” suddenly resolves to a public package of the same name with a higher version. What is this attack?

choices.label: A hijacked maintainer account
A malicious install script
Dependency confusion
Typosquatting

questions.explanation: The resolver preferred the public registry’s higher version of an internal name. Typosquatting relies on a mistyped name, a hijacked maintainer publishes under the real package, and an install script attack needs no name clash.

questions.prompt: What does a lockfile with hashes give you?

choices.label: The same reviewed versions on every build
Encrypted dependencies
Faster package downloads
Automatic upgrades to the newest security patches

questions.explanation: Builds stop drifting to new, unreviewed releases.

questions.prompt: What does a software bill of materials (SBOM) list?

choices.label: The tests that passed
The servers and regions that run the release
The components and versions in a release
The people who wrote each line

questions.explanation: An SBOM is an inventory you can match against new vulnerability reports.

questions.prompt: Signed build provenance says an image was built by your CI from commit abc123. What does verifying it at deploy stop?

choices.label: Images built elsewhere being deployed
A compromised CI runner signing its own build
Bugs in commit abc123
Vulnerabilities in dependencies

questions.explanation: Provenance ties an artefact to your trusted build. It cannot detect a compromised builder that signs its own output, bugs in the commit, or vulnerable dependencies; those need hardened builders, review and scanning.

questions.prompt: Order a verifiable release pipeline.

items.label: Resolve dependencies from the lockfile
Build in an isolated CI runner
Verify the signature before deploying
Sign the artefact and its provenance

questions.explanation: Pin, build cleanly, sign, verify.

questions.prompt: A critical vulnerability is announced in a logging library. Leadership asks which of 300 services are affected.

approaches.label: Query SBOMs generated for every release
Ask every team to check by hand
Scan production servers file by file

rationaleOptions.label: Answers in minutes with exact versions
Scanning files is as precise as an inventory
Covers transitive dependencies teams may not know about
Teams know their dependencies well enough

rationaleConflicts.r3: Most affected copies arrive as transitive dependencies.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Shaded and bundled copies are easy to miss.

questions.explanation: An inventory made at build time answers “are we affected?” quickly.

flashcards.back: A public package with an internal package’s name gets installed instead.
An inventory of components and versions in a release.
Signed, verifiable metadata about how and where an artefact was built.
