mechanism.title: Securing source, build and dependencies
steps: Source: protect the repository with required reviews and protected branches, and require strong authentication for maintainers. A single compromised account that can push to main without review undoes every later control.

Dependencies: pin exact versions with hashes in lockfiles, prefer a curated internal mirror, scope internal package names so public registries cannot shadow them, and update deliberately with automated pull requests that run tests.

Build: run builds in ephemeral, isolated CI environments defined in code, not on a developer laptop. The build should not have production secrets, and its outputs should be stored in a registry that records digests.

Provenance: SLSA, an industry framework, defines build levels. Level 1 means provenance exists describing how the artefact was built; level 2 means it is signed by a hosted build platform; level 3 means the build platform is hardened so even project maintainers cannot forge provenance.
Verification: signatures and provenance only help if checked. Admission controls at deploy time can refuse images that are unsigned or were not built from the expected repository.

Inventory and response: an SBOM per release lets you match a new vulnerability to affected services in minutes. Vulnerability scanners on those SBOMs feed the update process, prioritised by whether the vulnerable code is reachable.

useWhen: Use lockfiles, an internal mirror and CI-only builds.
Use signed provenance and verify at deploy.
avoidWhen: Avoid building releases on personal machines.
Avoid auto-merging dependency updates without tests.

rows: A malicious version you chose to pin
Compromise of the CI system itself

numbers.title: How many packages do you trust?
assumptions: A service lists 40 direct dependencies; each pulls in about 15 transitive ones (illustrative)
Each package has on average 2 maintainers with publish rights
steps: Total packages: 40 + 40 × 15 = 640.
Accounts that can publish code you run: about 640 × 2 = 1,280.
If each account had a 1-in-10,000 chance of compromise per year, the chance at least one is compromised is about 1 − (1 − 0.0001)^1,280 ≈ 12% a year.
Pinning, review of updates and provenance reduce how much a single compromised account can reach you.
numbers.result: Transitive dependencies multiply the people and accounts you implicitly trust.

india.title: The xz backdoor
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: Publicly reported in March 2024 (CVE-2024-3094): a contributor who had spent about two years gaining maintainer trust in the xz compression project added a backdoor to release tarballs of versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1, hidden in test files and build scripts rather than the visible source. On some Linux distributions it could compromise SSH servers. An engineer noticed SSH logins using unusual CPU time, investigated, and disclosed it before the versions reached most stable releases.

pitfalls.trap: “We only use well-known packages.”
pitfalls.say: “Well-known packages are high-value targets too; I’d pin versions and verify what we build.”

pitfalls.trap: “Our scanner shows no CVEs, so dependencies are safe.”
pitfalls.say: “Scanners find known issues; a new backdoor has no CVE yet, so provenance and review still matter.”

takeaways: Pin dependencies with hashes; scope internal names.
Build only in isolated CI; sign and verify artefacts.
Keep an SBOM per release to answer “are we affected?”
Assume transitive code runs with your permissions.

choices.label: The deploy key leaks before any test runs
choices.feedback: Right: install scripts run immediately with the runner’s permissions.

choices.feedback: Install-time scripts execute during installation.

choices.feedback: The exfiltration happens before tests start.

title: Multi-Factor Authentication and Phishing Resistance
objectives: Compare SMS codes, authenticator apps, push approvals and passkeys
Explain why origin binding makes passkeys phishing-resistant
Design recovery without creating a weaker back door

cards.title: Factors add independent proof
cards.body: Multi-factor authentication combines things you know (password), have (phone, security key) and are (biometric unlocking a device). An attacker who steals a password still needs the second factor, which stops most automated account takeover.

cards.title: Not all second factors are equal
cards.body: SMS codes can be intercepted or redirected by SIM swapping. Authenticator-app codes (TOTP) avoid the phone network but can be typed into a phishing site. Push approvals can be spammed until a tired user taps “approve”. Passkeys and security keys are bound to the real site and resist phishing.

cards.title: Worked example: how a TOTP code is made
cards.body: An authenticator app and the server share a secret set up by scanning a QR code.
steps: Both sides take the current Unix time and divide by 30 seconds to get a counter
Each computes HMAC-SHA1(secret, counter)
They truncate the result to a 6-digit code
The server accepts the code for the current step and usually one step either side for clock drift
It records the used code so the same one cannot be replayed

cards.title: Misconception: any MFA stops phishing
cards.body: A real-time phishing proxy shows the victim the genuine login page through the attacker’s server and relays the password and one-time code as they are typed, then keeps the session cookie. Codes do not know which site they were typed into; WebAuthn credentials do.

cards.title: Trap: account recovery that skips MFA
cards.body: If “lost your phone?” resets the account with only an email link or a support call, attackers target that path instead. Recovery should require comparable assurance: backup codes, a second registered key, or identity checks with delays and notifications.

questions.prompt: Which factor resists a real-time phishing proxy?

choices.label: A passkey bound to the site’s origin
A 6-digit SMS code
A 6-digit authenticator code
A code sent in an email that expires quickly

questions.explanation: WebAuthn signs a challenge tied to the real origin; codes can be relayed.

questions.prompt: A user receives 30 push approval requests at 2 a.m. and finally taps approve. What attack is this?

choices.label: MFA fatigue
Session fixation
Credential stuffing
SIM swapping

questions.explanation: Repeated prompts wear the user down; number matching and rate limits help.

questions.prompt: Why do TOTP servers accept a code one step either side of now?

choices.label: To let a code be reused once
To allow for clock drift
To resist phishing of the code
To lower the chance of guessing

questions.explanation: Phone clocks drift and users take time to type, so a one-step window accepts valid codes. It slightly widens the guessing window, does nothing against phishing, and servers should still reject a reused code.

questions.prompt: What makes SMS the weakest common second factor?

choices.label: Phone numbers can be hijacked by SIM swap
Codes are too short to type
SMS needs an internet connection
Codes can be guessed in a few tries

questions.explanation: Attackers persuade carriers to move the number to their SIM, then receive the codes. Six-digit codes with rate limits are not practically guessable, and SMS needs no internet connection.

questions.prompt: Order a passkey sign-in.

items.label: Server verifies the signature with the stored public key
User unlocks the authenticator with a fingerprint or PIN
Server sends a random challenge
Authenticator signs the challenge with the key for that origin
Browser checks the site’s origin and asks the authenticator

questions.explanation: Challenge, origin check, user verification, sign, verify.

questions.prompt: An internal admin console controls production and has been targeted by phishing campaigns.

approaches.label: Require passkeys or hardware security keys for the console
Push approvals without number matching
SMS one-time codes

rationaleOptions.label: Nothing to relay or approve by mistake
Credentials only work on the genuine origin
SMS is fine because staff phones are trusted
Push approvals are phishing-proof

rationaleConflicts.r3: SIM swaps and phishing proxies bypass the phone’s security.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Users can approve a login they did not start.

questions.explanation: For high-value access, use factors bound to the origin.

flashcards.back: Something you know, have, or are.
The browser binds each credential to the site’s origin.
HMAC of a shared secret and a 30-second time counter, truncated to digits.

mechanism.title: Why origin binding beats one-time codes
steps: One-time codes (SMS, TOTP, email) are secrets the user reads and types. Anything the user can type, a phishing page can collect and replay within the code’s 30-second to few-minute window.

WebAuthn (behind passkeys and security keys) creates a key pair per site. Registration stores the public key on the server. At sign-in the server sends a challenge; the browser includes the site’s origin in what the authenticator signs, and refuses to use a credential for any origin other than the one it was created for.

Because the origin is enforced by the browser, a look-alike domain cannot request a signature for the real site. A phishing proxy receives a signature for its own origin, which the real server rejects. This is what “phishing-resistant” means in NIST’s guidance.

Passkeys are WebAuthn credentials that can be synced across a user’s devices by their platform, which solves the lost-device problem that held back hardware keys, at the cost of trusting the sync provider’s account security.

Push approvals sit in between: number matching (typing the number shown on the login screen into the app) and showing location and app details reduce fatigue attacks, but the user can still approve a session they did not start. NIST SP 800-63B-4 cites authentication fatigue and no longer accepts a bare approve tap: the user must transfer a secret between the devices, which number matching does when the user types the number shown on screen into the app; picking it from a short list does not count.

Recovery and enrolment are part of the system. Require MFA to add or remove factors, notify on changes, issue single-use backup codes, and make help-desk resets slower and verified, since attackers move to the weakest path.

useWhen: Use passkeys or security keys for admins, production access and other high-value accounts.
Use TOTP or number-matched push as a baseline for everyone else while passkeys roll out.
Use notifications on every factor change so users spot takeovers.
avoidWhen: Avoid SMS where stronger options exist.
Avoid recovery flows weaker than sign-in.

rows: User may approve an attacker’s login

numbers.title: How long a stolen TOTP code is usable
assumptions: 30-second step, server accepts the current and previous step (illustrative)
Phishing proxy relays codes within 2 seconds
steps: A code is valid for at most about 60 seconds.
The proxy needs 2 seconds, well inside the window.
Shortening the step to 15 seconds still leaves 13 seconds or more of margin.
The window is not the weakness; the lack of origin binding is.
numbers.result: Shorter codes do not beat real-time phishing; binding the credential to the origin does.

india.title: Prompt bombing at a ride-hailing company
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: Publicly reported by Uber in September 2022: an attacker who had obtained a contractor’s password repeatedly sent multi-factor push approval requests, and the contractor eventually accepted one, giving the attacker access to internal systems. The incident became a widely cited example of MFA fatigue and pushed many companies towards number matching and phishing-resistant authenticators for employees.

pitfalls.trap: “We have MFA, so phishing is solved.”
pitfalls.say: “Codes and pushes can be relayed or approved by mistake; for critical systems I’d require passkeys or security keys.”

pitfalls.trap: “SMS is fine as a backup.”
pitfalls.say: “Attackers target the weakest enrolled factor, so the backup sets the real security level.”

takeaways: MFA blocks most password-only attacks.
Codes and pushes can be phished or fatigued.
Passkeys and security keys are bound to the origin.
Recovery must be as strong as sign-in.

choices.label: No: the browser will not use the real site’s passkey on another origin

choices.feedback: There is nothing to relay; the signature names the proxy’s origin.

choices.label: Yes, if the user confirms with a fingerprint
